why_how.text: An officer directing traffic can overrule the signals, so officer directions come first.
Each steady light, and each arrow, carries its own duty for the driver.

scenario.text: Mia approaches an intersection just as the light turns steady yellow, and she is too close to stop safely.

reasoning.text: At a steady yellow, you stop before the intersection unless you are too close to stop safely.

result.text: Mia continues through with care, because stopping safely is no longer possible.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a green light means you never have to yield.

correction.text: On green you still yield to pedestrians and vehicles in the intersection, and to oncoming traffic before a left turn.

memory_support.text: Red top, red left, officer first.

prompt.text: The light is green and Ravi wants to turn left. Whom must he yield to?

answer.text: Oncoming vehicles, plus pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection.

rationale.text: A green light lets you go ahead, but you yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection, and before a left turn you yield to oncoming vehicles.

narration.text: This lesson is about traffic signals and the people who can override them. A police officer directing traffic can overrule the traffic signals, and a driver must always obey law enforcement orders and directions. After that, we go light by light: how signals are arranged, what a steady red and a steady yellow require, what a yellow arrow warns about, how green still involves yielding, and what a green arrow allows. We also cover pedestrian push buttons and the penalties for damaging signs and signal equipment. By the end, each light should bring one clear duty to mind.

Signals follow a fixed order. On a vertical signal, red is always on top, yellow is in the middle and green is third, with any green arrow at the bottom. On a horizontal signal, red is always on the left. Learn that order as a fixed pattern for both layouts. Signals and signs are also protected. Stealing or damaging airport, traffic or railroad-crossing signs or equipment brings court penalties. So the equipment that keeps you safe is treated seriously, and tampering with it is a court matter. On a horizontal signal, then, the left position is always where you find red.

lines.text: Red: stop, stay stopped until green.

narration.text: At a red light, stop before the intersection or crosswalk and stay stopped until the light turns green. A steady yellow light asks you to stop before entering the intersection or crosswalk, unless you are too close to stop safely. Notice the difference in the two duties. Red is absolute: you stop before the intersection or crosswalk and you wait for green. Yellow is a judgment: you stop if you safely can, and you continue only when stopping safely is no longer possible. In both cases, the stopping point is before the intersection or the crosswalk, never inside it.

lines.text: Steady yellow: stop unless too close.

narration.text: Two yellow signals sound alike but say slightly different things. A steady yellow light means stop before entering the intersection or crosswalk unless you are too close to stop safely. A yellow arrow warns that the light is about to go from green to red, giving you time to stop safely. So the yellow arrow is a warning about the change that is coming for the movement it points to. A question might claim that a yellow arrow lets you turn freely. It does not; it tells you the light is about to turn red, and the safe response is to prepare to stop.

On a green light, go ahead, but yield to pedestrians and vehicles still in the intersection, and before turning left, yield to oncoming vehicles. A green arrow, alone or together with a red light, lets you go only in the direction the arrow points, and you still yield to pedestrians. Pedestrian push buttons can change the timing too. At signals with push buttons, pressing the button soon changes the flow so the side street gets a longer green. So green never removes the duty to yield, and an arrow gives permission only for the direction it shows.

Here is a quick check: Ravi reaches an intersection on a steady green light and wants to turn left. A pedestrian is still finishing a crossing, and an oncoming car is approaching. Ravi thinks green means he simply goes. Whom must he yield to? Work it out before reading on. Ravi must yield to the pedestrian and to any vehicles still in the intersection, and before turning left he must yield to the oncoming vehicle. A green light lets you go ahead, but it never removes the duty to yield. If an officer were directing traffic, Ravi would follow the officer instead.

Let us review. A police officer directing traffic can overrule the signals, and you always obey law enforcement directions. On a vertical signal red is on top, then yellow, then green, with any green arrow at the bottom, and on a horizontal signal red is on the left. At a steady red you stop and stay stopped until green. At a steady yellow you stop unless too close. A yellow arrow warns that red is coming. On green you still yield, especially before a left turn, and a green arrow lets you go only its way. Damaging signs or signal equipment brings court penalties.

why_how.text: Flashing lights and dark signals change what a normal signal would ask of you.
Pedestrian signals tell walkers when to start and tell turning drivers to yield.

scenario.text: Ana reaches an intersection where every signal bulb is dark and no one is directing traffic.

reasoning.text: A signal with no working bulbs and no one directing traffic must be treated as a four-way stop.

result.text: Ana stops and treats the intersection as a four-way stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a flashing red light only means slow down.

correction.text: Flashing yellow means slow down and take care; flashing red means a full stop before going on when safe.

memory_support.text: Yellow flashes slow, red flashes stop.

prompt.text: Ana's intersection has a flashing yellow light. What does it ask of her?

answer.text: Slow down and proceed with care.

rationale.text: A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care, while a flashing red would require a full stop.

narration.text: Not every signal shows a steady red, yellow or green. In this lesson we look at signals that flash, signals that go dark, and the signals that speak to pedestrians. A flashing yellow and a flashing red sound similar, but they ask for very different actions. A signal with no working bulbs has its own rule. And the pedestrian signals, the raised palm and the walking figure, tell walkers what to do while also reminding turning drivers whom to yield to. Keep asking the same question for each one: does this signal ask me to slow down, or to stop?

A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care. A flashing red light means stop, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and go only when it is safe. So the flashing yellow never requires a stop by itself, while the flashing red always does. After stopping at a flashing red, you yield to traffic and pedestrians and then go when it is safe. A flashing yellow asks for something different: slow down and proceed with care, without a required stop. At a flashing red you yield to both traffic and pedestrians, and only then do you go on.

Here is the swap that catches learners. A flashing yellow light only asks you to slow down and take care, but a flashing red light requires a full stop before going on when safe. A question may describe a flashing red and offer slow down as the answer, or describe a flashing yellow and offer a full stop. Keep one pairing in mind: flashing yellow means slow and take care, flashing red means stop. And after the stop at a flashing red, you go on only when it is safe. A flashing red never lets you roll through without stopping, while a flashing yellow never demands a stop by itself.

lines.text: Treat it as a four-way stop.

narration.text: Sometimes a signal stops working entirely. A signal with no working bulbs and no one directing traffic must be treated as a four-way stop. That gives every driver the same duty to stop, then go when it is safe. Do not treat a dark signal as a green light for the busier road. The rule applies only when no one is directing traffic. If a police officer is there, the officer's directions take over, just as they can overrule a working signal. So the order is: officer first, working signal second, and a dark signal becomes a four-way stop.

lines.text: Raised palm: do not step off.

narration.text: Pedestrian signals speak to walkers, but drivers need to understand them too. When pedestrians face a steady orange raised palm, they must not step off the curb, and anyone already in the crosswalk will have time to finish crossing. On a steady white walking figure or a countdown, pedestrians may cross, and New Jersey law requires turning drivers to yield to them. So when you are turning and the walking figure is lit, expect people in the crosswalk and give way. When the raised palm appears, people already crossing may still be finishing, so stay alert before you turn.

Here is a quick check: Ana approaches an intersection where the signal is flashing yellow. Her passenger says she has to come to a full stop and wait. What does the flashing yellow actually ask of her? Work it out before reading on. It asks her to slow down and proceed with care. A full stop is required at a flashing red light, where she would stop, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and go only when safe. If the signal had no working bulbs at all and no one was directing traffic, she would treat the intersection as a four-way stop.

Let us wrap up. A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care. A flashing red light means stop, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and go only when safe. A signal with no working bulbs and no one directing traffic is treated as a four-way stop. For pedestrians, a steady orange raised palm means do not step off the curb, while those already crossing have time to finish. A white walking figure or countdown means pedestrians may cross, and New Jersey law requires turning drivers to yield to them. Next, we move from lights to the shapes and colors of signs.

why_how.text: Shapes and colors let you recognize a sign's job before you read it.
The manual reserves specific shapes and colors for specific messages.

scenario.text: Leo sees a five-sided yellow sign ahead while driving through town.

reasoning.text: A yellow pentagon, with five sides, marks a school sign, unlike the three-sided pennant for no passing.

result.text: Leo recognizes a school sign and drives with that in mind.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the three-sided shapes, the red YIELD triangle and the yellow no-passing pennant.

correction.text: The red triangle is for YIELD signs, while the yellow pennant marks a no-passing zone warning.

memory_support.text: Eight STOP, three YIELD, five school.

prompt.text: Leo spots a yellow pennant on the left side of the road. What does it mark?

rationale.text: A yellow pennant, a three-sided shape, marks a no-passing zone; the five-sided yellow pentagon marks a school.

narration.text: Signs talk to you through shape and color before you read a single word. In this lesson we start with the three categories of signs, then learn the shapes the manual reserves for particular messages: the octagon, the triangle, the pennant and the pentagon. After that come the colors: orange for construction and maintenance, yellow diamonds for warnings, and blue, brown and green for services, recreation and directions. Learning these pairings means you can tell a sign's job from a distance. Several of the shapes have three sides or similar colors, so watch for the details that separate them.

Signs fall into three categories. Warning signs alert you to hazards that are hard to see. Guidance signs identify routes and destinations. Regulatory signs control speed and movement. Each category answers a different question. A warning sign asks you to prepare for something ahead. A guidance sign helps you find your way. A regulatory sign tells you what you must or must not do. When a question asks which kind of sign controls your speed, the answer is regulatory. When it asks which kind tells you where a route goes, the answer is guidance.

Now the shapes. A red octagon, with eight sides, is used only for STOP signs. A red triangle, with three sides, is used for YIELD signs. A yellow pennant, also a three-sided shape, marks a no-passing zone warning. A yellow pentagon, with five sides, marks a school sign. Count the sides and note the color together. Eight sides in red means STOP and nothing else. Three sides in red means YIELD. Three sides in yellow, in the pennant shape, means no passing. Five sides in yellow means a school. Those four pairings are worth memorizing as a set.

Here is where shapes collide. Both the YIELD sign and the no-passing warning are three-sided. The red triangle is used for YIELD signs. The yellow pennant marks a no-passing zone warning. So when you think three sides, the color decides the meaning: red means yield, yellow means no passing. A question might describe a yellow three-sided sign and offer yield as the answer. That would be wrong; a yellow pennant warns of a no-passing zone. And do not let the yellow pentagon join the confusion: it has five sides and marks a school.

Diamonds come in two key colors. An orange diamond warns of construction and maintenance work. General warning signs are yellow diamonds with a black symbol or word message. The yellow diamond is also used for roadway hazard and railroad crossing warning signs. So orange tells you work is going on, while yellow carries the everyday warnings about the road itself. Both are warnings, which fits the category of signs that alert you to hazards that are hard to see. The color tells you whether the hazard comes from work on the road or from the road ahead.

Rectangular signs in three colors help you find things rather than warn you. Blue rectangular signs give motorist services and information. Brown ones point to public recreation and scenic areas. Green ones give direction guidance. These belong with the guidance idea of identifying routes and destinations. A quick way to keep them apart is to tie each color to what you would be looking for: services and information on blue, a park or scenic stop on brown, and the road to your destination on green. Warnings, by contrast, come on the diamond-shaped signs.

Here is a quick check: Leo is driving on a two-lane road when he spots a yellow sign with three sides in the pennant shape. His friend says it must be a YIELD sign because yield signs have three sides. Is the friend right? Work it out before reading on. The friend is not. A red triangle is used for YIELD signs, but a yellow pennant, also three-sided, marks a no-passing zone warning. Leo should not pass in that zone. If the sign had five sides and was yellow, it would be a pentagon marking a school sign instead. The color and the number of sides together give the answer.

Let us review. Signs are warning, guidance or regulatory. The red octagon, with eight sides, is only for STOP. The red triangle is for YIELD. The yellow pennant marks a no-passing zone, and the yellow pentagon marks a school. An orange diamond warns of construction and maintenance, and yellow diamonds with black symbols or words are general warnings, also used for roadway hazards and railroad crossing warnings. Blue rectangles give motorist services, brown ones point to recreation and scenic areas, and green ones give directions. Next, we look closer at warning signs and work zones.

why_how.text: Warning signs prepare you for curves, people on foot or bike, and road work.
Work zones bring special rules, from doubled fines to flaggers with real authority.

scenario.text: Sam drives into a road work area where a flagger signals him to stop.

reasoning.text: A flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, so disobeying one can lead to a citation.

result.text: Sam stops as directed and watches for workers and moving machinery.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a flagger's signal is only a suggestion.

correction.text: A flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, and a driver who disobeys one can be cited.

memory_support.text: Work zone: fines double, flaggers rule.

prompt.text: Sam ignores a flagger's stop signal in a work zone. What can happen?

rationale.text: A flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, so a driver who disobeys one can be cited.

narration.text: Warning signs give you time to prepare. In this lesson we cover advisory speed signs on curves and turns, the warning signs for pedestrian crossings and bicycles, and the orange signs that mark road work. Work zones carry several rules of their own: reduced speed limits, doubled traffic fines in New Jersey, and flaggers who have the authority of a regulatory sign. We finish with the orange triangle that marks a slow-moving vehicle. Throughout, notice that warnings ask for preparation: slowing, watching, and being ready to stop.

When the safe speed on a curve or turn is lower than the posted limit, an advisory speed sign is posted with the warning sign. That advisory speed tells you what is safe for that curve, even though the posted limit is higher. Other warnings are about people. Pedestrian crossing and bicycle warning signs may be standard yellow or an optional yellow-green, and they tell drivers to share the road with and yield to pedestrians and cyclists. So a yellow-green sign is not a different rule; it carries the same message to share the road and yield.

Orange diamond road work signs warn of lane closings, lane shifts, flaggers, uneven pavement and detours. Reduced speed limit signs are posted alongside orange work zone signs. And in New Jersey, all traffic fines double in work zones. So an orange sign is your cue that the road ahead is changing and the cost of a mistake has gone up. Near road work, control your following distance and reaction time, read and follow the signs, be ready to slow or stop, and watch for workers and moving machinery. Each of those habits matches a hazard that the orange signs warn about.

lines.text: Disobey and you can be cited.

narration.text: Here is a trap about authority. Some drivers treat a flagger as a helpful guide whose signals can be ignored if the road looks clear. The manual says otherwise: a flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, so a driver who disobeys one can be cited. Recall that regulatory signs control speed and movement. A flagger's stop or slow signal works the same way. Combine that with doubled traffic fines in New Jersey work zones, and ignoring a flagger can be costly. Follow the flagger exactly as you would follow a regulatory sign.

One warning travels on vehicles rather than on posts. A fluorescent, reflective orange triangle on the back of a vehicle marks a slow-moving vehicle, such as farm or construction equipment on a public highway. Do not confuse it with the orange diamond, which warns of construction and maintenance work ahead. The triangle tells you the vehicle in front of you is a slow-moving vehicle. The diamond tells you construction or maintenance work is happening. Both are orange, but one is a shape on a vehicle and the other is a road sign.

Here is a quick check: Sam is driving through a road work area. A flagger signals him to stop, but the lane ahead looks empty, so Sam thinks he can keep going. What can happen if he does? Work it out before reading on. Sam can be cited. A flagger has the same authority as a regulatory sign, so disobeying one is like ignoring a regulatory sign. On top of that, all traffic fines double in New Jersey work zones. Sam should stop as directed, be ready to slow or stop, and watch for workers and moving machinery. A citation is possible because the flagger's signal carries the authority of a regulatory sign.

Let us wrap up. An advisory speed sign is posted with a curve or turn warning when the safe speed is lower than the posted limit. Pedestrian and bicycle warning signs, in yellow or optional yellow-green, tell you to share the road and yield. Orange road work signs warn of lane closings, shifts, flaggers, uneven pavement and detours, reduced speed limits are posted alongside them, and all traffic fines double in New Jersey work zones. A flagger has the authority of a regulatory sign. A fluorescent orange triangle on the back of a vehicle marks it as slow-moving.

why_how.text: Regulatory signs control speed and movement, so recognizing their designs matters.
A few regulatory signs have distinctive designs worth knowing by sight.

scenario.text: Kim drives a delivery truck and sees a red national truck sign at a ramp.

reasoning.text: Red national truck signs mark where trucks are prohibited or where designated routes end.

result.text: Kim does not take the ramp and looks for a green truck sign showing where trucks are allowed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every truck sign means trucks are welcome.

correction.text: Green truck signs mark where trucks are allowed; red ones mark where trucks are prohibited or routes end.

memory_support.text: Green trucks go, red trucks don't.

prompt.text: Kim's truck reaches a ramp with a red national truck sign. May she take it?

answer.text: No, a red truck sign marks where trucks are prohibited or a route ends.

rationale.text: Green national truck signs mark routes and ramps where trucks are allowed, while red ones mark where trucks are prohibited or designated routes end.

narration.text: Regulatory signs are the ones that control speed and movement, so they carry the rules you must follow. In this short lesson we cover what most regulatory signs look like, the distinctive design of the YIELD sign, the design of the DO NOT ENTER sign, and the green and red national truck signs. Several of these use white and red together, so the details of shape and layout are what tell them apart. Learning the designs helps you recognize a rule before you read the words. Each design here follows the manual's description, so focus on the shape, the colors and where the words sit.

Regulatory signs are usually vertical rectangles with black wording and border on a white background. That plain design is the most common look for a rule on the road. Compare it with the colors you have already learned. Yellow diamonds are warnings, orange diamonds mean construction, and blue, brown and green rectangles help you find services, recreation and directions. A white vertical rectangle with black words is usually telling you what you must or must not do. Because regulatory signs control speed and movement, treat a white rectangle as a rule to obey, not just information.

lines.text: YIELD: white inverted triangle, red border.
DO NOT ENTER: red circle, white band.

narration.text: Two regulatory signs mix red and white in distinctive ways. A YIELD sign is a white inverted triangle with red wording and a red border inside a white border band. A DO NOT ENTER sign is a white square holding a red circle crossed by a horizontal white band, with the words in white above and below the band. So the YIELD sign is a triangle pointing down, while the DO NOT ENTER sign is a square with a red circle inside it. Recall too that the red triangle shape itself is the one used for YIELD signs. The red circle and white band belong to DO NOT ENTER, and the downward-pointing triangle belongs to YIELD.

Truck drivers, and anyone answering a question about trucks, need to keep two colors straight. Green national truck signs mark routes and ramps where trucks are allowed. Red national truck signs mark where trucks are prohibited, or where designated routes end. A question might show a red truck sign and suggest it marks a truck route. That is backwards. Think of a traffic light: green means go, so trucks may use that route or ramp; red means stop, so trucks may not, or the designated route has ended. The same sign shape carries opposite rules depending on color.

lines.text: Red truck sign at a ramp.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Kim drives a delivery truck and reaches a highway ramp marked with a red national truck sign. She assumes any truck sign means the ramp is meant for trucks. Should she take the ramp? Work it out before reading on. She should not. Red national truck signs mark where trucks are prohibited or where designated routes end. Green national truck signs are the ones that mark routes and ramps where trucks are allowed. Kim should look for a route or ramp marked with a green truck sign instead of taking the ramp with the red one.

lines.text: YIELD and DO NOT ENTER designs.

narration.text: Let us review. Regulatory signs are usually vertical rectangles with black wording and border on a white background. A YIELD sign is a white inverted triangle with red wording and a red border inside a white border band. A DO NOT ENTER sign is a white square holding a red circle crossed by a horizontal white band, with the words in white above and below the band. Green national truck signs mark routes and ramps where trucks are allowed, while red ones mark where trucks are prohibited or where designated routes end. Next, we turn to railroad crossings.

why_how.text: Trains cannot swerve, so drivers must always yield at railroad crossings.
Crossings use both signs and active devices, and each kind tells you something different.

scenario.text: Omar stops at a crossing where the red lights have just stopped flashing, but the bells are still ringing.

reasoning.text: You may go only after the lights stop flashing and every other active warning device shuts off.

result.text: Omar waits until the bells stop as well, then crosses when it is safe.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may cross as soon as the flashing red lights stop.

correction.text: You must also wait until every other active warning device, such as bells or gates, shuts off.

prompt.text: The crossing lights stopped flashing, but the bells still ring. May Omar go?

answer.text: Not yet; he waits until every active warning device shuts off.

rationale.text: Flashing red lights at a crossing mean a train is coming, and you may go only after they stop and every other active warning device shuts off.

narration.text: Railroad crossings get their own lesson because the stakes are high and the rules are firm. Drivers must always yield to trains, because trains cannot swerve. In this lesson we cover the white X and the round yellow advance sign, what the crossbuck means, what flashing red lights at a crossing mean and when you may go, and the difference between passive and active warning devices. Each of these is a way the road tells you a train may be near. Your job is to recognize every one of them and give the train the right of way.

A round yellow sign is the advance warning that a railroad crossing is ahead, and a white X marks the railroad crossing itself. The crossbuck, a white X-shaped railroad sign with black lettering, means the same as a Yield sign, and drivers must always yield to trains because trains cannot swerve. So the round yellow sign gives you early notice, and the crossbuck at the tracks tells you to yield. Recall that the yellow diamond is also used for railroad crossing warning signs, so railroad warnings can reach you in more than one form before the tracks.

lines.text: Flashing red: a train is coming.
Wait for every device to stop.

narration.text: Here is the trap at crossings. Flashing red lights at a railroad crossing mean a train is coming, and you may go only after they stop flashing and every other active warning device shuts off. Many drivers watch only the lights. If the lights stop but the bells are still ringing, you are not yet free to go. The same is true if a gate is still lowered. Active warnings include flashing red lights, ringing bells and lowered gates, and every one of them must be off before you cross. Treat any active device that is still working as a sign that a train may be coming.

Railroad warnings fall into two groups. Pavement markings, signs and crossbucks are passive railroad warning devices. Flashing red lights, ringing bells and lowered gates are active warnings. Passive devices are always there, telling you a crossing exists and that you must yield to trains. Active devices switch on when a train is coming. So at a crossing with only passive devices, you still yield to trains. At a crossing with active devices, you also wait for every one of them to shut off. In both cases, the train has the right of way because it cannot swerve.

Here is a quick check: Omar is stopped at a railroad crossing. The flashing red lights have just gone dark, but the bells are still ringing. The driver behind him honks, so Omar wonders whether he may go. What should he do? Work it out before reading on. Omar should wait. You may go only after the flashing red lights stop and every other active warning device shuts off. Ringing bells are an active warning, so the crossing is not clear yet. Once the bells stop too, Omar may cross when it is safe, still yielding to any train.

Let us review. A round yellow sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead, and a white X marks the crossing. The crossbuck, a white X-shaped sign with black lettering, means the same as a Yield sign, and you must always yield to trains because they cannot swerve. Flashing red lights at a crossing mean a train is coming, and you may go only after they stop and every other active device shuts off. Pavement markings, signs and crossbucks are passive warnings, while flashing lights, ringing bells and lowered gates are active warnings. Next come the lines painted on the road.

why_how.text: Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and signals.
Line color tells you about traffic direction, and line pattern tells you about passing.

scenario.text: Pat drives on a two-lane road with a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line side by side, the dashed line on Pat's side.

reasoning.text: With combined lines, you may pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and you must finish before the dashes turn solid.

result.text: Pat passes when it is safe and returns to the lane before the dashed line turns solid.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking road markings are only suggestions compared with signs.

correction.text: Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and traffic signals.

memory_support.text: Yellow opposes, white follows, dashes pass.

prompt.text: Pat sees combined yellow lines with the solid line on Pat's side. May Pat pass?

answer.text: No, passing is allowed only when the dashed line is on your side.

rationale.text: With a solid and a dashed yellow line side by side, pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and finish before the dashes turn solid.

title.text: Lines with the force of law

narration.text: Painted lines are easy to take for granted, but road markings carry the same force of law as signs and traffic signals. In this lesson we learn what line colors mean, what dashed and solid lines mean for passing, how to read a solid and a dashed line side by side, and what double solid lines require. We also cover road arrows, the white dashed lines between lanes on multi-lane highways, and edge lines. Two questions unlock most markings: which way is the traffic on the other side of this line moving, and does the pattern on my side allow passing?

Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, while white lines separate lanes moving the same way and mark road edges. So a yellow line on your left tells you that traffic beyond it is coming toward you. A white line beside you tells you the traffic in the next lane is moving your way. On multi-lane highways, white dashed lines separate the lanes. Edge lines separate the shoulder from the travel lane and mark the edge of the highway, and yellow edge lines do the same job. Road arrows used with other signs show the direction you must take from that lane.

lines.text: Dashed on your side: may pass.
Solid on your side: may not.

narration.text: The pattern of the line on your side of the center line decides whether you may pass. A dashed line on your side means you may pass when it is safe. A solid line on your side means you may not pass. Notice the phrase on your side. Many roads use two lines together, and what matters is the line closest to your lane. Even with a dashed line, passing is allowed only when it is safe. So the dashed line gives permission, but your judgment about traffic and visibility still decides whether passing is safe at that moment.

lines.text: Dashed on your side: pass, finish early.
Solid on your side: no pass.

narration.text: Here is the trap with combined lines. With a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line side by side, pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and finish the pass before the dashes turn solid. If the solid line is on your side, you may not pass, even though a dashed line is right next to it. Double solid yellow and white lines prohibit passing. Never cross a solid yellow line to pass, stay in your lane, and keep right when driving slowly. So the rule always comes back to the line nearest your lane, and double solid lines mean no passing at all.

A few more markings guide your lane choice. Road arrows used with other signs show the direction a driver must take from that lane, so if your lane's arrow points left, that lane is for going left. White dashed lines separate lanes on multi-lane highways. Edge lines separate the shoulder from the travel lane and mark the edge of the highway, and yellow edge lines do the same job. Because road markings carry the same force of law as signs and signals, an arrow in your lane is a rule, not a suggestion, and the edge line marks where the travel lane ends.

Here is a quick check: Pat is driving on a two-lane road behind a slow vehicle. The center has a solid yellow line and a dashed yellow line side by side, and the solid line is on Pat's side. The road ahead looks clear. May Pat pass? Work it out before reading on. Pat may not. With combined lines, you pass only when the dashed line is on your side, and you finish before the dashes turn solid. With the solid line on Pat's side, passing is not allowed, so Pat stays in the lane until the markings change. The solid line nearest Pat's lane is what decides the answer.

lines.text: Dashes on your side to pass.

narration.text: Let us review. Road markings carry the same force of law as signs and signals. Yellow center lines separate opposite directions, and white lines separate same-direction lanes and mark road edges. A dashed line on your side means you may pass when safe, and a solid line on your side means you may not. With combined lines, pass only with the dashed line on your side and finish before the dashes turn solid. Double solid lines prohibit passing. Road arrows show the direction from your lane, white dashed lines split highway lanes, and edge lines separate the shoulder from the travel lane.

why_how.text: Special markings warn of conditions ahead and show exactly where to stop.
Some road features slow you, wake you, or change how an intersection works.

scenario.text: Jo approaches a stop sign at a corner where no stop line is painted but a crosswalk is marked.

reasoning.text: Where no stop line is painted, stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires you to stop.

result.text: Jo stops before the crosswalk, not in it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking rumble strips can damage your vehicle.

correction.text: Rumble strips vibrate the wheel and make noise as a warning, and they do not damage the vehicle.

memory_support.text: Bump short, hump long, strips rumble.

prompt.text: Jo must stop for a sign at a corner with a crosswalk but no stop line. Where does Jo stop?

rationale.text: Where no stop line is painted, you stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires a stop; where a white stop line exists, you stop at it.

narration.text: This last lesson collects special markings and road features. We start with where to stop when there is a stop line and when there is not. Then we cover white words painted on the pavement, such as STOP AHEAD, and the white diamonds that mark high occupancy vehicle lanes. After that we compare speed bumps, speed humps and rumble strips, three features that you feel through the car. We finish with the roundabout, a kind of intersection designed to reduce severe crashes. Each of these features gives you information through the road surface itself.

lines.text: White stop line: stop at it.
No stop line: before the crosswalk.

narration.text: Stopping in the right place matters. Where a white stop line exists, stop at it. Where no stop line is painted, stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires you to stop. So the order of choices is simple. If there is a stop line, that is your mark. If there is no stop line but there is a crosswalk, you stop before the crosswalk, never in it. Remember that a sign, a signal or a pedestrian can each create the duty to stop, so the stopping point rule applies whichever of the three is asking you to stop.

title.text: Words and diamonds on the road

narration.text: Some markings use words. White special pavement markings such as STOP AHEAD, SCHOOL and RXR alert drivers to special conditions ahead. Other markings use a symbol. White diamonds on signs or painted in the lane mark high occupancy vehicle lanes, known as HOV lanes, reserved for certain vehicles or for vehicles carrying several riders, and posted signs give the operating hours. So a painted word warns you about what is coming up, while a white diamond tells you who may use that lane. Do not confuse white diamonds with yellow diamond signs, which carry general warnings.

Three features you feel in the car are easy to mix up. A speed bump is a low ridge across the street. A speed hump is a longer, flatter version. Rumble strips are different again: they vibrate the wheel and make noise to warn of a decision point ahead or to wake a dozing driver, they do not damage the vehicle, and they usually come with a caution sign. So bumps and humps are ridges across the street, while rumble strips are a warning you hear and feel. A question that mentions vibration and noise is describing rumble strips, not a bump or hump.

lines.text: Enter and exit by right turns.

narration.text: A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection around a center island. Because traffic enters and exits only by right turns, severe crashes are greatly reduced. Those two facts belong together: the one-way flow and the right-turn entry and exit are the reason the design is safer. So when you use a roundabout, you travel one way around the island, and you enter and leave by turning right. A question that suggests entering a roundabout with a left turn, or driving both directions around the island, does not match the manual's description of how a roundabout works.

Here is a quick check: Jo approaches a stop sign at a corner. A crosswalk is painted across the street, but there is no white stop line. Jo is unsure whether to stop at the sign, in the crosswalk, or past it. Where should Jo stop? Work it out before reading on. Jo should stop before the crosswalk. Where no stop line is painted, you stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires you to stop. If a white stop line had been painted, Jo would stop at the line instead. Either way, the stop comes before the crosswalk, never inside it.

Let us review. Stop at a white stop line, and where none is painted, stop before the crosswalk when a sign, signal or pedestrian requires a stop. White pavement words such as STOP AHEAD, SCHOOL and RXR alert you to special conditions ahead, and white diamonds mark HOV lanes, with posted signs giving the hours. A speed bump is a low ridge, a speed hump is longer and flatter, and rumble strips vibrate and make noise as a warning without damaging the vehicle. A roundabout is a one-way circle entered and exited by right turns, which greatly reduces severe crashes.
